title: AIs Historical Present Same Chair Different Gap November 9, 2026
author: Jessica Maddry
source: Educating AI (nickpotkalitsky.substack.com), guest post in the AI’s Historical Present series,
summary: Jessica Maddry, a former science teacher and co-founder of an advisory that helps K-12 districts understand their data privacy and AI governance, tells how she used Claude to turn a hand-built research process into a prototype app. Her idea was to show district leaders what story their online information tells to families, partners and bots. She did the research by hand like grading a stack of student papers, then had Claude design a report and later help build a working prototype. When she checked the output against what she already knew, it missed leadership changes, board questions, the existence of a CTO and AI policy details, so the polished report looked complete but was not. Repeated correction produced a repeatable snapshot process that cut research time. Her central point is that her expertise made the project possible and let her spot what looked right but was wrong, yet she could not verify the back end, so she brought in an AI developer.
points: Domain expertise is what lets a non-technical educator design a useful AI process and recognise when an output only looks complete, much like checking a student paper.
A polished AI-built report or prototype can be missing key facts, so every output has to be checked against what you independently know.
Gaps in the prototype pointed to the next piece of work rather than a reason to abandon it, and iterative correction turned the idea into a repeatable, defensible process.
AI cut research time drastically so that human effort could go to review and verification.
Knowing when a project has moved beyond your own expertise, and bringing in a developer to stress-test the back end, is part of responsible building.
quotes: The report looked complete, but it was not. That was the moment when the excitement gave way to something more familiar: the student paper that looks finished until you slow down and actually check the work.
Each time the prototype missed something, I returned to my original process. I compared what the app found with what I knew could be found.
Still, the educator in me understood that a gap is not a reason to abandon the work. A gap tells you where the work needs to go next.
My expertise gave me the idea and the insight needed to design the process. Without that expertise, there would have been no meaningful conversation with AI.
I could recognize a problem in the result, but I could not guarantee that the machine behind it would continue producing the right result.

Closing a gap has never meant pretending I can do everything myself. It means seeing clearly enough to know what I can contribute, what I still need to learn, and when another person belongs in the work.
